objectives: Explain how a trucking company generates revenue
Describe how a fleet is structured and identified
Tell the difference between a tractor and a trailer
body: A trucking company moves freight for customers. A shipper needs goods moved from point A to point B; the carrier supplies a truck, a trailer and a driver, and gets paid for the load — usually by the mile or by the load. Every hour a truck cannot run is an hour it cannot earn. That single fact is why maintenance coordination exists.

The collection of vehicles a company operates is its fleet. Each vehicle is an asset tracked by a unit number (for example T-114 for a tractor or TR-532 for a trailer). Unit numbers are how everyone — drivers, dispatch, shops and you — refer to equipment. Each unit also has a 17-character [[VIN]] that uniquely identifies the vehicle.

tiles.title: Tractors (power units)
tiles.text: The truck that has the engine, cab and drive axles. Sleeper tractors have a bed for long-haul drivers; day cabs are used for local work.

tiles.title: Trailers
tiles.text: Carry the freight. Common types: dry van (enclosed box), reefer (refrigerated), flatbed, tanker.

tiles.title: Drivers
tiles.text: Assigned to a tractor, hauling different trailers load to load. They are your eyes and ears on the road.

tiles.title: Terminals & yards
tiles.text: Company locations where equipment is parked, dispatched and sometimes repaired in an in-house shop.

body: A tractor and trailer are separate vehicles with separate unit numbers, separate maintenance schedules and separate repair histories. They connect through the [[Fifth wheel]] on the tractor, which locks onto the trailer's [[Kingpin]]. Air lines (connected with [[Glad hands]]) and an electrical cord carry brake air and lighting power from tractor to trailer.

head: Tractor
Trailer
rows: No (except a reefer unit's small engine for cooling)
Tires, brakes, lights, doors, landing gear, reefer unit
Mileage/time; reefer units also by hours

callout.title: Why it matters to you
callout.text: When a driver says "the truck has a problem," your first job is to confirm which unit — tractor or trailer — and its unit number. Opening a case on the wrong unit corrupts repair history.

industry.name: Pro Transport USA
industry.text: Pro Transport, Inc. describes itself as a trucking and transportation provider founded in 1998, with its corporate office in Medley, Florida and terminals in Florida, Georgia and South Carolina. It serves local, regional and national customers with employees and owner-operators.
industry.relevance: A carrier like this is the structure this lesson describes: terminals, tractors, trailers and drivers moving freight for customers. Every unit in a fleet like this needs the maintenance coordination you're learning here.

example.title: One load, many moving parts
example.text: A driver in tractor T-114 picks up trailer TR-532 loaded with retail goods in Dallas, delivering to Atlanta tomorrow at 08:00. If T-114 develops a problem, the load can sometimes be saved by sending another tractor to pull TR-532. If TR-532 has a problem, the load itself may be stuck. Knowing which unit is affected changes your entire plan.

practical.title: Read a unit assignment

msg.title: Dispatch board entry
msg.text:
Driver: M. Reyes   Tractor: T-114   Trailer: TR-532 (Dry van)
Load #48213   PU: Dallas, TX 06/12 14:00   DEL: Atlanta, GA 06/13 08:00

blocks: Before any maintenance call, a coordinator glances at this line and knows: who is driving, which two units are involved, what the load is, and when it is due. If the driver reports "a trailer tire is low," you immediately know the case belongs to TR-532, not T-114, and that there is a delivery deadline at 08:00.

check.q: Why does downtime matter so much to a trucking company?
o: Trucks lose value faster when parked
A truck that cannot run cannot earn revenue
Drivers are paid more when trucks are down
Parked trucks require more insurance
check.e: Trucks earn money by moving freight. Every hour of downtime is lost earning capacity — this is the core reason maintenance coordination exists.

check.q: A tractor and the trailer it is pulling share the same unit number and repair history.
check.e: They are separate assets with separate unit numbers, maintenance schedules and repair histories. Always confirm which unit has the issue.

takeaways: Trucking revenue depends on equipment moving — downtime is lost revenue.
Every vehicle is tracked by a unit number and a 17-character VIN.
Tractors provide power; trailers carry freight. They are separate units with separate histories.
Always identify the exact unit before opening a maintenance case.
tips: Keep the dispatch board open — it tells you who, what unit, what load and what deadline in one line.
Learn your fleet's unit-number pattern (e.g., T- for tractors, TR- for trailers) so you catch typos instantly.
mistakes: Opening a case on the tractor when the problem is on the trailer.
Forgetting that a stuck trailer means a stuck load — even if another tractor is available.

blocks.title: Trailer types and their maintenance footprint
blocks.hint: More dots = more. Reefers add a refrigeration unit with its own engine; tankers can require specific tests depending on cargo.

blocks: Different trailer types bring different maintenance needs. A reefer failure can spoil a load; a tanker may carry products with special handling and inspection requirements; flatbeds depend on securement equipment the driver uses every day.

blocks.title: Operating cost of a long-haul truck (illustrative)
blocks.note: Illustrative shares to show scale. Maintenance is a meaningful slice — and downtime affects every other slice because the costs continue while revenue stops.

objectives: Identify the key roles in a trucking company
Explain what each department needs from maintenance
Describe how departments interact during a breakdown
body: A Maintenance Coordinator sits at the center of several departments. You rarely turn a wrench, but you connect the people who do — and the people who depend on the truck being ready.

tiles.title: Driver
tiles.text: Operates the vehicle, performs pre-trip and post-trip inspections, reports defects. Primary source of information about a problem.

tiles.title: Dispatcher
tiles.text: Assigns loads to drivers and tracks them to delivery. Needs to know if and when a truck can move.

tiles.title: Maintenance Coordinator
tiles.text: Receives maintenance issues, arranges repairs with the right vendor, tracks progress and communicates status. Owns the case.

tiles.title: Fleet Manager
tiles.text: Responsible for the fleet as a whole: budgets, policies, vendor relationships, equipment decisions. Approves larger repairs.

tiles.title: Technician
tiles.text: Diagnoses and repairs the vehicle — in-house or at an outside shop. The person qualified to make mechanical decisions.

tiles.title: Parts Department
tiles.text: Sources, stocks and tracks parts. Knows lead times and alternatives.

tiles.title: Safety Department
tiles.text: Ensures compliance with regulations (inspections, driver qualifications, hours of service) and investigates incidents.

tiles.title: Operations
tiles.text: The broader team that plans capacity, customer commitments and daily execution. Maintenance decisions affect their plan.

body: During a typical breakdown, information flows in a loop. The driver reports to you (or to dispatch, who routes it to you). You gather facts, decide urgency and arrange a vendor. Dispatch needs your ETA so they can protect the load. The technician needs your complaint details. The fleet manager needs to approve anything outside your authority. Safety needs to know if the event involves a safety-critical defect or regulatory issue.

callout.title: You are the hub
callout.text: Most delays in maintenance come from information not reaching the right person. Your value is making sure each party knows what they need, when they need it.

example.title: Who needs to know?
example.text: Driver R. Chen calls: the trailer ABS warning light is on. You open a case on the trailer, arrange an inspection at a shop near the route, and then: tell dispatch the expected delay, tell the shop the complaint and unit details, and — because ABS is a brake-system issue — follow your company procedure, which may include notifying the safety department.

practical.title: Map the conversation

dialog: Hey, my check engine light just came on. Truck seems fine though.
Thanks for calling it in. Which unit are you in, and where are you right now?
T-120, I'm on I-40 eastbound near mile marker 212.
You open a case on T-120, then contact a shop and notify dispatch of a possible delay.

blocks: Notice how the coordinator starts with identification (unit, location) before troubleshooting. Every department downstream depends on those two facts.

check.q: Who is qualified to make the final mechanical diagnosis of a problem?
o: The Maintenance Coordinator
The Dispatcher
The Technician
The Driver
check.e: Technicians diagnose and repair. The coordinator gathers information and coordinates — but does not make mechanical diagnoses.

check.q: A tractor will be in the shop for 6 hours. Which department most urgently needs your ETA?
o: Parts
Dispatch
Safety
Accounting
check.e: Dispatch must decide whether the load can still make its appointment, needs a recovery truck, or requires the customer to be notified.

takeaways: The coordinator connects drivers, dispatch, vendors, parts, safety and management.
Technicians make mechanical decisions; coordinators make coordination decisions.
Dispatch depends on your ETAs to protect loads and customer commitments.
Unit number and location are always the first two facts you collect.
tips: Save direct lines for your most-used shops and dispatchers — minutes matter on roadside calls.
When two departments want different things, write down both needs before you decide.
mistakes: Letting dispatch learn about a delay from the driver instead of from you.
Giving a shop only "check engine light" when the driver told you much more.

objectives: Tell FTL, LTL and partial loads apart
Explain live loading vs drop and hook
Recognize how cargo type changes the urgency of a repair
Read axle-group weights against U.S. limits
body: Every unit you coordinate is either carrying freight, going to get freight, or waiting for it. What kind of load is on the truck changes who is affected by a breakdown, how fast you need to move, and which vendor can help.

body.title: How freight fills a trailer: FTL vs LTL vs partial

items.sub: One shipper's freight uses the trailer.
items.watch: A breakdown delays one customer, but the whole trailer — recovery often means a tractor swap.

items.sub: Many shippers' freight shares one trailer.
facts: Freight class (NMFC classes 50–500), weight and distance
items.watch: Linehaul schedules between terminals: a late trailer can miss its departure and delay every shipment on it.

items.sub: More than typical LTL, less than a full trailer.
facts: Often shares a trailer with another partial; few stops
items.watch: Multiple appointments on one trip — a delay affects every stop.

body.key: The load type tells you how many customers a breakdown affects and whether the freight can wait.

body.title: Live load vs drop and hook

items.sub: The driver and tractor wait at the dock while freight is loaded or unloaded.
facts: Free time, then detention per the rate agreement
Tractor and trailer tied up together
items.watch: A no-start at the dock blocks the customer's door — these calls are urgent even when the fix is simple.

items.sub: The driver drops one trailer and hooks a preloaded one.
facts: Usually much faster for the driver
Needs more trailers than tractors (a trailer pool)
items.watch: Trailers sit in customer yards for days. Defects surface at pickup — plan trailer PMs and inspections so pooled trailers don't fall behind.

body.key: Live loads tie up the tractor; drop-and-hook ties up trailers. Both change where and when you can schedule maintenance.

body.title: Cargo types and what changes for maintenance

items.sub: No temperature control.
items.watch: Standard urgency — the freight can usually wait for a repair.

items.sub: Setpoint from the shipper's instructions.
items.watch: Reefer faults are time-critical. Keep the unit running and cargo in range while you arrange service.

items.sub: Regulated under 49 CFR Parts 171–180 (U.S. DOT / PHMSA).
facts: Table 1 materials: any amount. Table 2: 1,001 lb or more aggregate
Hazmat (H) endorsement when placards are required
items.watch: Leaks, fire risk and vendor qualifications. Follow your safety department's procedure before arranging any repair.

items.sub: Beyond legal size or weight limits.
facts: State permits set routes, travel times, signs/flags and escorts — rules vary by state
items.watch: A breakdown can push the move outside its permitted route or hours. Involve dispatch or the permit team immediately.

body: Trucks are limited in total (gross) weight and in weight per axle group. A load can be under 80,000 lb and still be overweight on one axle group — usually fixed by adjusting the trailer tandem slide or re-working the load.

body.title: Weight per axle group: gross weight isn't the only limit
body.note: U.S. federal Interstate limits: 34,000 lb per tandem axle group and 80,000 lb gross (23 CFR 658.17), subject to the bridge formula; states set rules for other roads and permits. The 12,000 lb steer figure is a common axle/tire rating used here for illustration, not a federal limit. Sliding the trailer tandem generally shifts weight between the drives and trailer axles; sliding the fifth wheel shifts it between the steer and drives — the driver confirms at a scale.

body.title: Cargo securement basics (U.S. — 49 CFR 393 Subpart I)
head: Rule
Requirement
Source
rows: Tiedowns together must be rated for at least 50% of the cargo weight
Article 5 ft or shorter, 1,100 lb or less
Article 5 ft or shorter over 1,100 lb, or 5–10 ft long
2 tiedowns for the first 10 ft, plus 1 for each additional 10 ft or part of 10 ft
Within the first 50 miles, then at every change of duty status, or every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first
body.note: Tiedown counts apply when an article is not blocked against forward movement; commodity-specific rules (logs, metal coils, heavy equipment and others) add requirements. Summary for orientation only — the regulation and your safety department are the authority.

callout.title: Who decides?
callout.text: Load legality, weight and securement are the driver's, dispatch's and the safety department's responsibility. The coordinator's part is knowing that these conditions change the urgency of a repair and the vendor you call — for example, a flatbed breakdown with a strap failure, or a reefer alarm with a temperature-sensitive load.

example.title: Same breakdown, three different urgencies
example.text: Three tractors lose an alternator on the same morning. T-201 is hauling a dry van of paper towels due tomorrow — you schedule a repair on the route. T-214 is live-unloading at a grocery DC and won't restart — the customer's dock is blocked, so you call a mobile tech now and tell dispatch. T-230 pulls a reefer with ice cream — the reefer runs on its own engine, so the cargo is safe for now, but you confirm the unit's fuel level and temperature before choosing between a mobile repair and a power swap.

items.text: Freight from nine shippers moving through a terminal
items.why: Many shippers sharing a trailer through terminals is LTL.

items.text: One shipper's 26 pallets, picked up and delivered direct
items.why: One shipper using the whole trailer.

items.text: 10 pallets sharing a trailer with another 10-pallet shipment, two delivery stops
items.why: Larger than typical LTL, less than a full trailer, few stops.

items.text: Priced by freight class, weight and distance
items.why: Freight class (NMFC) pricing is an LTL feature.

items.text: Trailer sealed at the shipper, opened only at the consignee
items.why: No stops or rehandling in between.

check.q: What is the U.S. federal Interstate limit for a tandem axle group?
check.e: 34,000 lb per tandem group; 20,000 lb per single axle; 80,000 lb gross — subject to the bridge formula (23 CFR 658.17).

check.q: What does drop and hook require that live loading doesn't?
o: A hazmat endorsement
More trailers than tractors
A reefer unit
A step deck
check.e: Preloaded trailers wait for drivers, so the fleet needs a pool of extra trailers.

check.q: A truck under 80,000 lb gross can still be overweight.
check.e: Axle-group limits apply separately. Too much weight on the drives is illegal even when the gross is fine.

takeaways: FTL = one shipper; LTL = many shippers through terminals; partial = in between.
Live loads tie up the tractor; drop and hook ties up trailers.
Reefer, hazmat and oversize loads raise the urgency and narrow the vendor list.
Weight limits apply per axle group as well as in total.
tips: On every breakdown call, ask "loaded or empty — and with what?" before choosing a plan.
For pooled trailers, schedule inspections when a trailer is empty in your own yard.
mistakes: Treating a reefer load like dry freight because the tractor issue "isn't urgent."
Assuming that under 80,000 lb gross means the truck is legal.

objectives: List the daily responsibilities of a Maintenance Coordinator
Explain what "owning a case" means
Describe how a coordinator monitors the fleet
body: A Maintenance Coordinator keeps equipment safe and moving by managing maintenance events from start to finish. You are measured on how quickly and correctly equipment returns to service — and on how well everyone stays informed along the way.

timeline.title: Monitoring vehicles
timeline.text: Watch fleet status: open repairs, upcoming PMs, fault code alerts from telematics, and units that are down.

timeline.title: Receiving maintenance requests
timeline.text: Requests arrive by phone, message, driver inspection reports (DVIRs), telematics alerts or from dispatch.

timeline.title: Understanding driver complaints
timeline.text: Ask structured questions to turn a vague report into a clear description of the problem.

timeline.title: Opening a maintenance case
timeline.text: Create a record (case or work order) with the unit, complaint, location, mileage, time and urgency.

timeline.title: Finding repair facilities
timeline.text: Identify a qualified vendor near the unit: in-house shop, dealer, independent shop, mobile service or tow.

timeline.title: Coordinating repairs
timeline.text: Send complaint details to the shop, confirm arrival, obtain diagnosis and estimate, and route approvals per company procedure.

callout.title: Owning the case
callout.text: Once you open a case, you are responsible for it until it is closed. That means following up without being asked, updating every stakeholder, and never letting a unit "sit" without a next step.

body.title: A coordinator's morning — work runs in parallel
body.note: Illustrative schedule. The skill is keeping several open cases moving at once without losing any of them.

example.title: A morning on the desk
example.text: At 07:10 a telematics alert shows T-131 logged a low coolant level fault. At 07:25 a driver reports a trailer door that will not latch. At 07:40 dispatch asks when T-108 will be out of the shop. A coordinator handles all three — opening cases, prioritizing by safety and load impact, and chasing updates — while keeping notes on each.

items.why: Watching alerts and fleet status is monitoring.

items.text: Driver calls: trailer door won't latch
items.why: A new request coming in from a driver is intake.

items.text: Calling the shop for T-108's diagnosis and estimate
items.why: Working with a vendor on an existing repair is coordination.

items.text: Reviewing which units are due for PM next week
items.why: Tracking upcoming maintenance is fleet monitoring.

check.q: What does "owning a case" mean?
o: You pay the repair invoice from your department's budget once approved
You are responsible for the case until it is closed, including follow-up and communication
You must inspect the vehicle in person before any vendor may start work
You choose which parts and brands the technician installs on each repair
check.e: Ownership means accountability for the case's progress and communication until it is closed.

check.q: Maintenance requests only come from drivers calling in.
check.e: Requests also come from inspection reports, telematics alerts, dispatch, PM schedules and shops.

takeaways: Coordinators monitor the fleet, take in requests, and coordinate repairs.
Every issue becomes a documented case with a clear owner.
Requests come from many channels — drivers, DVIRs, telematics, dispatch.
A case never sits without a next step.
tips: Start every shift with a fleet review: units down, ETRs due today, PMs due this week.
Write the next follow-up time on every open case before you move on.
mistakes: Working cases strictly in the order they arrived instead of by urgency.
Relying on memory for open cases instead of a written list.

industry.text: Fleetio is fleet management software. Its website describes it as "one place to run fleet maintenance," aimed at reducing downtime and controlling costs, for fleets in industries including trucking and freight.
industry.relevance: Much of a coordinator's day happens inside fleet maintenance software: opening cases, logging work orders, tracking PM schedules and reviewing unit history.

blocks.title: Four questions to place any new request

blocks: Answer these four before anything else. They decide whether the case jumps the queue, gets same-day service, or goes on the schedule.

objectives: Explain why downtime must be tracked
Describe effective follow-up habits
Distinguish what a coordinator does and does not do
body: Opening the case is the easy part. The work that separates a strong coordinator from an average one happens after the truck reaches the shop.

timeline.title: Tracking downtime
timeline.text: Record when the unit went down, arrived at the shop, was diagnosed, repaired, and released. Downtime is one of the most watched numbers in a fleet.

timeline.title: Following up
timeline.text: Set a follow-up time on every open case. Shops are busy; a polite, timely check-in keeps your unit moving.

timeline.title: Updating operations
timeline.text: Push status changes to dispatch without waiting to be asked: diagnosis received, parts ordered, ETA changed, unit released.

timeline.title: Closing cases
timeline.text: Confirm the repair is complete, the driver has the unit, and the complaint is resolved — then close.

timeline.title: Documentation
timeline.text: Every step is written down: who you talked to, what was decided, times, costs and results.

body.h: What a coordinator does — and does not do

yes.title: Does
items: Routes estimates for approval per company procedure

no.title: Does not
items: Diagnose mechanical problems or tell a technician how to repair
Tell a driver to keep operating a vehicle with a safety defect
Guess at information that should be confirmed
Leave a case without a next action

callout.title: Never override safety
callout.text: Pressure to "just get the load delivered" is common. A coordinator never instructs a driver to operate a vehicle that the driver, a technician or regulations consider unsafe.

body.title: The life of a maintenance case
body.note: Every status change is a moment to update dispatch and write a time-stamped note.

example.title: Silent cases cost money
example.text: A shop received T-108 Monday morning. Nobody followed up. Wednesday, dispatch asked for an ETA — the shop had been waiting since Monday afternoon for approval on the estimate. Two days of downtime came from a missing phone call, not a mechanical problem.

practical.title: Set a follow-up rhythm

head: Case stage
Typical follow-up
rows: Confirm ETA of technician; check again at ETA
Confirm check-in and expected diagnosis time
Check at the promised time; escalate if missed
Confirm part ETA and tracking; check daily
Confirm ETR; update dispatch on any change

blocks: Company procedures differ — but the principle is the same: every open case has a scheduled next touchpoint.

check.q: A shop promised a diagnosis by 14:00. It is 14:45 and you have heard nothing. What do you do?
o: Wait — they will call when ready
Call the shop, get a status, and update dispatch with any change
Tell dispatch the truck will be ready at 17:00
Send the truck to a different shop immediately
check.e: Follow up proactively, get facts, then communicate. Never invent an ETA, and don't move a unit without reason.

check.q: A coordinator should tell the technician which part to replace based on the driver's description.
check.e: Diagnosis belongs to the technician. The coordinator passes along the complaint details clearly and accurately.

takeaways: Downtime tracking starts the moment a unit goes down.
Every open case has a scheduled follow-up.
Update dispatch proactively — don't wait to be asked.
Coordinators coordinate; technicians diagnose; safety is never negotiable.
tips: Update dispatch at each status change — not only at the end.
Before closing, ask the driver directly: "Is the problem gone?"
mistakes: Closing a case when the shop says "done" but before the driver confirms.
Leaving a case in "diagnosed" for hours while an approval waits in your inbox.

blocks.title: Touchpoints on a same-day shop repair

objectives: Identify the main powertrain components
Understand what the cooling, fuel and exhaust systems do
Recognize aftertreatment components and why they matter
body: You do not need to be a mechanic — but you do need to understand what a technician is talking about. Explore the interactive diagram, then read the system summaries below.

accordion.title: Engine
accordion.text: Most heavy trucks use a diesel engine. It turns fuel into power. Engine issues show up as warning lights, loss of power, smoke, unusual noise, or leaks.

accordion.title: Transmission
accordion.text: Transfers engine power to the drivetrain through gears. Many modern trucks use automated manual transmissions (AMTs). Issues: failure to shift, grinding, warning messages, stuck in gear.

accordion.title: Driveshaft & differential
accordion.text: The driveshaft carries power to the rear axles. The differential lets the wheels on each side turn at different speeds in turns. Issues: vibration, clunking, whining, leaks.

accordion.title: Cooling system
accordion.text: Radiator, coolant, water pump, thermostat, fan and hoses keep the engine at operating temperature. Overheating can severely damage an engine.

accordion.title: Fuel system
accordion.text: Tanks, lines, filters, pumps and injectors deliver diesel to the engine. Issues: hard starting, loss of power, fuel leaks, contaminated fuel.

accordion.title: Exhaust & aftertreatment
accordion.text: Modern diesels clean exhaust with a Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF), Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) using Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF), and often Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR). Faults here commonly cause engine derates (reduced power).

callout.title: Aftertreatment in one sentence
callout.text: The [[DPF]] traps soot and periodically burns it off ("regeneration"); the [[SCR]] system injects [[DEF]] to convert NOx into nitrogen and water; [[EGR]] recirculates some exhaust to lower combustion temperature. Problems in any of these can trigger a derate.

example.title: The derate call
example.text: A driver reports the truck "won't go over 5 mph" and there is a message about DEF. You don't need to fix it — but because you know DEF feeds the SCR system and that aftertreatment faults commonly trigger derates, you ask the right follow-ups: Is the DEF level low? Any other warning lights? Is the truck in a safe place? That information gets the right vendor there faster.

practical.title: Translate the technician

dialog: We found the DPF differential pressure sensor reading high. Truck couldn't complete a regen. We're going to do a parked regen and replace the sensor.
Understood — so the filter wasn't cleaning itself because of a bad sensor reading. What's the ETR, and do you have the sensor in stock?

blocks: Knowing the vocabulary lets you ask the two questions that matter to operations: when will it be done, and is anything holding it up.

check.q: What does the DPF do?
o: Injects diesel exhaust fluid so the SCR catalyst can reduce NOx
Traps soot from exhaust and burns it off during regeneration
Cools recirculated exhaust gas before it returns to the intake
Measures exhaust temperature so the engine can adjust fuel timing
check.e: The Diesel Particulate Filter traps soot; regeneration burns the soot off.

check.q: A driver reports low power and a DEF warning. Which system is most likely involved?
o: Cooling
Aftertreatment
Steering
Suspension
check.e: DEF is part of the aftertreatment (SCR) system. Aftertreatment faults commonly cause derates.

takeaways: Engine, transmission, driveshaft and differential form the powertrain.
Cooling and fuel systems keep the engine running safely.
DPF, SCR/DEF and EGR make up aftertreatment — a frequent cause of derates.
Know enough vocabulary to ask about ETR and parts — leave diagnosis to technicians.

deep.title: How a diesel makes power
blocks: Diesels ignite fuel with the heat of compressed air — no spark plugs. That is why injectors, turbochargers (which pack in more air) and fuel quality matter so much to performance and emissions.

objectives: Understand how air brakes work at a basic level
Identify tire, suspension, steering and electrical components
Name the main trailer components
body: Heavy trucks use air brakes. A compressor builds air pressure stored in tanks; pressing the pedal sends air to brake chambers at each wheel. Parking/emergency brakes are held off by air pressure — if pressure drops too low, spring brakes apply. Trucks also have [[ABS]], which prevents wheel lock-up during hard braking.

callout.title: Brake issues are safety-critical
callout.text: Air leaks, low-air warnings, brakes that pull, grind or don't release, and brake warning lights all require immediate attention. Brake defects are a common reason vehicles are placed out of service during inspections.

body.title: Drum vs air disc brakes

items.sub: An S-shaped cam pushes brake shoes against the inside of a drum.
facts: Long the most common type on North American trucks and trailers
Slack adjusters keep the brake in adjustment as linings wear
items.watch: Out-of-adjustment brakes are a common inspection violation — ask why a brake keeps drifting.

items.sub: A caliper squeezes pads against a rotor.
facts: Increasingly common, especially on steer axles
Generally resists fade better; faster pad changes; higher purchase cost
items.watch: Pads and rotors are different parts from drum shoes — confirm the brake type before ordering or sending a vendor.

body.key: Both are air-operated and both are safety-critical. The brake type changes the parts, the labor, and which vendor can do the job.

tiles.title: Tires
tiles.text: Steer tires (front), drive tires (under the tractor's rear) and trailer tires. Watch for flats, blowouts, low pressure, uneven wear and damaged sidewalls.

tiles.title: Suspension
tiles.text: Air bags (air springs) or leaf springs support the load. Issues: leaning, air leaks, rough ride, broken springs.

tiles.title: Steering
tiles.text: Steering gear, linkage and tie rods. Issues: loose steering, pulling, vibration, hard steering. Always safety-critical.

tiles.title: Electrical & battery
tiles.text: Batteries, alternator, starter, wiring and lighting. Issues: no-start, dim lights, warning messages, trailer lights out.

example.title: "My trailer is leaning"
example.text: A driver says the trailer looks like it's leaning to one side. With basic knowledge you recognize this could be a suspension air leak or a failed air bag — potentially affecting handling. You ask: Is there an audible air leak? Did any warning appear? Is the trailer loaded? Then you arrange an inspection rather than letting the unit continue on a guess.

practical.title: Match the symptom to the system

exercise.prompt: Which system is most likely involved?

items.text: Low air warning buzzer keeps going off
items.why: Air pressure supplies the brake system; a low-air warning is a brake-system issue.

items.text: Trailer marker lights are out on the left side
items.why: Lighting is electrical — often a wiring or connector issue.

items.text: Visible bulge on the sidewall of a drive tire
items.why: A sidewall bulge indicates internal tire damage — a blowout risk.

items.text: Trailer sits noticeably lower on one side
items.why: Uneven ride height points toward suspension (air bag/leak).

check.q: On a truck with air brakes, what happens if air pressure drops too low?
o: Nothing — brakes are hydraulic
Spring brakes can apply automatically
The engine shuts off
The ABS light turns off
check.e: Spring (parking/emergency) brakes are held off by air pressure. If pressure drops too low they can apply.

check.q: Brake and steering issues should always be treated as safety-critical.
check.e: Both directly affect the driver's ability to control and stop the vehicle.

takeaways: Heavy trucks use air brakes; low-air situations are safety-critical.
Know tire positions: steer, drive and trailer.
Suspension, steering and electrical problems each have distinct symptoms.
Trailers have their own components — kingpin, glad hands, landing gear, lights, reefer.
tips: Ask "tractor or trailer?" first on every tire, brake and light complaint.
For tire calls, ask which axle, which side, and inside or outside dual.
mistakes: Treating a "small air leak" as minor — any air loss affects the braking system.
Assuming the trailer has the same maintenance history as the tractor pulling it.

deep.title: Brake adjustment
blocks: S-cam air brakes need to stay in adjustment: as linings wear, the brake chamber pushrod travels farther before the brakes apply. Automatic slack adjusters compensate, but they can fail — and brakes out of adjustment are among the most common roadside inspection findings.

callout.title: Why adjustment matters
callout.text: Brake problems, including brakes out of adjustment, are among the most frequent vehicle out-of-service findings at CVSA roadside inspections. Automatic slack adjusters shouldn't need routine manual adjustment — if one keeps drifting, the brake needs diagnosis, not just re-adjusting.

callout.title: What to ask the shop
callout.text: If brakes are found out of adjustment, ask why — worn components, a failing automatic slack adjuster, or an installation issue. Repeated adjustment on the same wheel is a repeat failure.

deep.title: Air-brake numbers to know
blocks: Drivers describe air problems in numbers. Knowing the normal range tells you how serious a call is before a technician arrives.

blocks.title: Air-brake pressures (typical U.S. tractor)

items.l: normal working range: the governor stops the compressor near the top and restarts it near the bottom
the low-air warning must come on before pressure drops below this
spring brakes start to apply on their own, which can stop the truck in a lane
of service brakes defective puts the vehicle out of service at a roadside inspection

blocks.note: Governor settings vary by manufacturer; the 60 psi warning comes from the federal brake standard (FMVSS 121), and some state CDL manuals teach 55 psi. The 20% rule is how FMCSA records the brake out-of-service violation (49 CFR 396.3(a)(1)). Adjustment limits depend on chamber type and size: see the table in 49 CFR 393.47(e).

callout.title: What the numbers mean on a call
callout.text: A low-air warning, a gauge that drops fast when the driver brakes, or a hiss that does not stop all mean the same thing: the truck stays parked and a brake-qualified technician comes to it. Do not ask the driver to "build air and try to make it."

objectives: Name the key gauges a driver may report
Explain what an abnormal reading means for urgency
Translate warning lamps into coordinator actions
body: Drivers often describe problems by what they see on the dash. If you understand the main gauges and lamps, you can judge urgency within seconds — and ask better follow-up questions.

body.title: Warning lamp color guide

stops.d: Information — a system is on or active.
Attention — diagnose soon; watch for any change.
Likely derate — get to a safe place; arrange prompt diagnosis.
Serious — stop safely as soon as possible.

body.note: Symbols vary by manufacturer; color is the most reliable first clue. Always ask the driver to read the exact message.

callout.title: Oil pressure, temperature and air come first
callout.text: A low oil pressure reading, a climbing temperature with steam, or a low-air warning each mean "stop safely" — they protect the engine and, in the case of air, the brakes.

body.h: Questions to ask about any gauge or lamp

ul: What exactly does the message or lamp say — and what color is it?
Is the reading steady, climbing, or falling?
Did anything else change at the same time — power, noise, smoke?
Is it the first time, or has it happened before?

example.title: "The needle is low"
example.text: A driver says "one of the needles is low." The coordinator asks which gauge. It's the voltmeter, and the battery lamp is on. The coordinator asks the driver not to shut the engine off yet (the truck may not restart), finds a shop 12 miles away that can test the charging system, and arranges for the driver to go straight there.

exercise.prompt: How urgent is each dashboard report?

items.text: Oil pressure warning with the gauge near zero
items.why: Low oil pressure can destroy an engine quickly.

items.text: Low DEF warning, driving normally
items.why: Refill at the next stop; if ignored, power limits follow.

items.text: Voltmeter reading low while driving, battery lamp on
items.why: Charging problem — the truck may not restart. Get it tested before shutting down if possible.

items.text: Air pressure dropping with a low-air warning
items.why: Brake-system air loss is safety-critical.

items.text: Fuel gauge at a quarter tank
items.why: A planning item for dispatch and the driver.

check.q: Why do tractors usually have two air pressure gauges?
o: One gauge reads the tractor tires, the other the trailer tires
They show the primary and secondary brake air circuits
One shows tank pressure, the other the air in the suspension bags
The second gauge is a spare in case the first one stops working
check.e: The air brake system has primary and secondary circuits, each with its own gauge.

check.q: A HEST (high exhaust system temperature) lamp during a regeneration is, by itself, a sign of a failure.
check.e: It indicates hot exhaust during regeneration at low speed — a caution to keep clear of flammable material, not a fault by itself.

takeaways: Oil pressure, coolant temperature and air pressure are the "stop now" gauges when abnormal.
Lamp color is the first clue; the exact message is the second.
Ask whether readings are steady, climbing or falling.
Some problems (charging) change what the driver should do before shutting down.
tips: Keep a photo reference of your fleet's dash layouts — makes and models differ.
Ask drivers to send a photo of the dash when safe.
mistakes: Treating every lamp the same.
Telling a driver to shut down with a charging fault before a plan is in place.

objectives: Identify common power units and axle configurations
Tell the main trailer types apart by sight
Explain how equipment type changes the vendor and urgency
body: Drivers and shops will describe equipment by type — "the 6x2 day cab," "the step deck," "the chassis." Knowing what each looks like and why it exists helps you ask the right questions and send the right vendor.

body.title: Power units: what pulls or carries the freight

items.sub: No sleeping compartment.
facts: Local and regional — driver home daily
Many stops, frequent coupling and uncoupling
items.watch: Brakes and clutch/transmission wear from stop-start work; fifth wheel and glad hands from frequent coupling.

items.sub: Sleeper berth behind the seats.
items.watch: Mileage-based PMs, aftertreatment, and cab comfort systems the driver lives with (HVAC, APU — auxiliary power unit — if equipped).

items.sub: Cab and cargo body on one chassis — no separate trailer.
facts: Class B CDL when GVWR is 26,001 lb or more
items.watch: Cargo body, doors and liftgate (if equipped) — plus the same brakes and tires as any truck.

items.sub: Also called a terminal tractor, spotter or yard dog.
facts: Moving trailers around yards, ports and warehouses
Hydraulic fifth wheel lifts the trailer
items.watch: Hydraulics and fifth wheel; very high engine hours compared with miles, so PMs are usually hour-based.

body.key: A tractor pulls a separate trailer; a straight truck carries the cargo on its own chassis. Knowing which one broke tells you whether the freight can be moved by swapping power.

body.title: Tractor axle configurations (driven wheels highlighted)

items.sub: Two axles — one driven rear axle.
facts: Local and regional work, lighter loads

items.sub: Three axles — both rear axles driven.
facts: The usual setup for heavy over-the-road tractors

items.sub: Three axles — only one rear axle driven.
facts: Lighter, can save fuel, but less traction on slippery roads
Highway fleets focused on fuel economy

body.key: The first number counts wheel positions (duals count as one); the second counts how many of them are driven. A 6x2 stuck on ice is a traction limit, not necessarily a defect — ask before you send a technician.

body.title: Enclosed trailers: dry van vs reefer

items.sub: Enclosed box, no temperature control. The most common trailer in truckload freight.
facts: 102 in (8.5 ft) — U.S. federal width limit
items.use: Retail, packaged goods, paper, parts — anything that doesn't need temperature control.
items.watch: Doors, hinges and seals; floor and roof damage; lights; tires; brakes; tandem slider pins.

items.sub: Insulated box plus a front-mounted refrigeration unit, commonly with its own diesel engine and fuel tank.
facts: Trailer miles + reefer unit engine hours
From the shipper's instructions on the load paperwork
Slightly less than a dry van (insulated walls)
items.use: Food, pharmaceuticals, flowers, chemicals — anything temperature-sensitive, hot or cold.
items.watch: Unit PMs by hours, alarms, unit fuel, door seals, and temperature records. A reefer failure with cargo aboard is time-critical.

body.key: Same box, different risk: a dry-van breakdown delays freight; a reefer failure can destroy it. Reefer units often need a refrigeration technician, not a trailer shop.

body.title: Open-deck trailers: how deck height changes what fits

items.sub: One flat deck (roughly 5 ft off the ground), loaded from the sides or top.
facts: Straps, chains and tarps — 49 CFR 393 Subpart I
items.watch: Deck boards, winches, stake pockets, worn straps/chains, lights, tires.

items.sub: Short upper deck over the kingpin, then a lower main deck.
facts: Lower deck carries taller cargo than a flatbed within the same height limit
items.use: Machinery and tall loads that would be over height on a flatbed.
items.watch: Low-profile tires (check stock before a roadside call), deck, ramps if equipped.

items.sub: Removable gooseneck (RGN) detaches so equipment can drive on from the front; very low well deck.
facts: Loads are often oversize/overweight and need state permits
items.watch: Gooseneck hydraulics or mechanism, extra axles, deck — and the permit conditions if a breakdown delays the move.

body.key: The lower the deck, the taller the cargo that fits under the height limit (dashed red line). The limit itself varies by state — commonly 13 ft 6 in — so drivers and dispatch check routes for tall loads.

body.title: Specialty equipment: tanker, intermodal chassis, doubles

items.sub: Carries liquids, gases or dry bulk.
facts: CDL tank vehicle (N) endorsement; hazmat (H) too if the load is placarded hazmat
Liquid surge; many tanks have baffles or compartments
items.watch: Valves, hoses, vapor recovery, wash records. Hazmat cargo tanks have periodic test and inspection requirements (49 CFR Part 180).

items.sub: A frame that carries a shipping container between ports, rail ramps and customers.
facts: Often a chassis pool or provider — not the carrier
items.watch: Lights, tires, brakes and twist locks. Confirm who provides the chassis before arranging a repair — that decides who authorizes and pays.

items.sub: Two short (about 28 ft) trailers joined by a converter dolly.
items.watch: The dolly is its own unit: tires, brakes, lights, drawbar eye and safety chains.

body.key: Each of these adds a party or a requirement: tank qualifications, a chassis owner, or a third unit (the dolly) that needs its own inspection and records.

pins.d: Hinges, seals, lock rods. A door that won't latch can stop a load.
The "ICC bar." Damage or missing parts are inspection violations.
Axles slide on a rail to adjust weight distribution; locking pins must engage.
Holes or bent posts let in water and weaken the box.
Supports the parked trailer. "Won't crank" is a common yard call.
Locks into the tractor's fifth wheel. Wear or damage is a coupling safety issue.
Air and electrical connections to the tractor.

body.note: Whether a part belongs to the tractor or the trailer decides which unit the case is opened on.

practical.title: Match the description to the trailer

items.text: Enclosed trailer with a diesel-powered unit on the front wall
items.why: The refrigeration unit is the giveaway.

items.text: Open deck; cargo held with straps and covered by tarps
items.why: One flat open deck, secured and tarped.

items.text: Two deck heights so taller machinery fits under the height limit
items.why: The lower main deck gains cargo height.

items.text: Carries liquid; the driver needs an N endorsement
items.why: The tank vehicle endorsement is N.

items.text: Enclosed box for palletized general freight, no temperature control
items.why: The most common trailer in truckload freight.

check.q: In a 6x4 tractor, how many axles are driven?
o: One
Two
Four
Six
check.e: Six wheel positions, four of them driven — both rear axles.

check.q: Main advantage of a step deck over a flatbed?
o: It is enclosed, so cargo is protected from weather and theft
It carries taller cargo under the same height limit
It needs fewer tiedowns because the low deck holds cargo in place
It is shorter, so it fits more loading docks than a flatbed
check.e: The lower main deck leaves more room under the height limit.

check.q: Reefer unit engine hours are tracked separately from trailer miles.
check.e: The refrigeration unit has its own engine and PM schedule, usually by hours.

takeaways: Day cabs work local; sleepers work long-haul; straight trucks carry cargo on their own chassis.
Axle configuration = wheel positions × driven positions.
Deck height decides how tall a load fits on open-deck trailers.
Reefers, tankers, chassis and dollies each bring their own vendor and questions.
tips: Keep a photo sheet of each trailer type your fleet runs, with the unit-number format.
Add the equipment type to every case title — "TR-532 reefer" beats "TR-532."
mistakes: Sending a trailer shop to a reefer unit fault.
Arranging a repair on an intermodal chassis before confirming who owns it.

objectives: Explain why steer, drive and trailer tires differ
Name the main parts of a tire
Read a tire size and load index
Apply U.S. tread-depth minimums by position
body: Tire calls are among the most common roadside events. You don't change tires — but a precise description of the position, size and damage gets the right tire to the right place on the first trip.

body.title: Steer, drive and trailer tires look different for a reason

items.sub: Front axle — steering and handling.
facts: Rib: grooves run around the tire
Regrooved tires aren't allowed on the front wheels of heavy trucks and tractors (49 CFR 393.75)

items.sub: Powered axles — traction.
facts: Lug/block pattern with deep side slots

items.sub: Free-rolling — carries load, no steering or power.

body.key: A tire that is legal on a drive or trailer axle can be illegal on the steer axle. Always record the exact position: steer, drive or trailer — axle, side, inside or outside dual.

pins.d: The rubber that touches the road. Depth is measured in the grooves in 32nds of an inch.
Stiffen the tread area. Belt separation shows up as bulges and vibration — remove from service.
Carries the size, load and DOT codes. Cuts, bulges or exposed cords are serious — the sidewall isn't repairable like the tread area.
Holds the air in a tubeless tire.
Steel wire bundle that seals the tire against the wheel.
Must match the tire's rim size exactly. Cracked wheels and loose lug nuts are separate, serious defects.

body.title: Reading a tire sidewall: 295/75R22.5 144/141L
parts: Tire width in millimeters, sidewall to sidewall.
Sidewall height as a percentage of width — 75% of 295 mm.
Wheel diameter in inches. Tire and wheel must match.
144 = 2,800 kg (about 6,170 lb) per tire used single; 141 = 2,575 kg (about 5,680 lb) per tire used in duals.
body.note: Other common sizes use an older format, like 11R22.5 (11 = nominal width in inches). The DOT code's last four digits show when the tire was made: "2324" = week 23 of 2024. Give the vendor the full size from the sidewall, not from memory.

body.title: Same depth, different verdict: tread depth by position
body.note: U.S. minimums under 49 CFR 393.75: 4/32 in for steer tires, 2/32 in for all other positions. 3/32 in is legal on a drive tire but not on a steer tire. Many fleets replace tires well before the legal minimum by policy.

body.title: Radial vs bias-ply construction

items.sub: Cords run straight across from bead to bead, with steel belts under the tread.
facts: The standard for modern highway truck tires
Flexible sidewall, stable tread: longer wear, lower rolling resistance

items.sub: Cords cross each other at alternating angles.
facts: Older design; still found on some specialty and off-road equipment
Stiff, tough sidewall; more heat and wear at highway speed

body.key: The "R" in the size tells you it's radial. Radial and bias tires shouldn't be mixed on the same axle.

body.title: Duals vs wide-base singles

items.sub: Two tires on each end of a drive or trailer axle.
facts: If one fails, the wheel end isn't left bare — but the partner is suddenly overloaded
Both tires must be matched in size and wear to share the load
items.watch: An underinflated inner dual overloads the outer one. After a flat, have the partner inspected too.

items.sub: One wide tire replaces each pair of duals (for example, 445/50R22.5).
facts: No partner tire — a failure leaves that wheel end with nothing
items.watch: Roadside stock is thinner in some areas. Keep your fleet's wide-base sizes in the tire vendor list.

body.key: With duals, the partner tire takes the whole load when one fails and must be inspected too; with a wide-base single there is no partner at all. Either way, the driver stops safely and a tire technician decides whether the unit can move.

callout.title: Steer tires are never "limp it in"
callout.text: A damaged, bulging or low steer tire affects steering control. The driver stops in a safe place and a qualified tire technician decides — never suggest driving on it to reach a cheaper vendor.

ul: Position: steer, drive or trailer; which axle; left or right; inside or outside dual
Full tire size from the sidewall (and wide-base or dual?)
What happened: flat, blowout, cut, bulge, low pressure
Is the wheel or anything else damaged?
Loaded or empty, and exact location

example.title: The second trip
example.text: A driver reported "a flat on the trailer." The vendor arrived with a standard 11R22.5 — but the trailer ran wide-base singles. The vendor had to leave and come back, adding three hours of downtime. A coordinator who asks for the sidewall size and "dual or single?" avoids the second trip.

exercise.prompt: Which tire position does each description fit best?

items.text: Rib tread on the front axle, handles steering
items.why: Steer tires use rib patterns for handling.

items.text: Deep lug tread under the tractor's rear axles
items.why: Lugs give traction on powered axles.

items.text: Free-rolling, often shallower rib tread
items.why: Trailer tires carry load but don't steer or drive.

items.text: Must have at least 4/32 in of tread in the U.S.
items.why: Other positions have a 2/32 in minimum.

check.q: In 295/75R22.5, what does 22.5 mean?
o: Tread depth
Rim diameter in inches
Load index
Width in inches
check.e: The last number of the size is the wheel (rim) diameter in inches.

check.q: A tire at 3/32 in meets the U.S. minimum on a steer axle.
check.e: Steer tires need at least 4/32 in. 3/32 in is legal only on other positions.

check.q: What is different about a flat on a wide-base single compared with a flat on one dual?
o: Wide-base tires cost less
There is no partner tire at that wheel end
Wide-base tires are only used on steers
Duals can't go flat
check.e: A wide-base single replaces the pair — when it fails, that wheel end has nothing.

takeaways: Tread pattern matches the job: rib to steer, lug to drive, free-rolling on trailers.
Read the size from the sidewall and give it to the vendor exactly.
Tread minimums differ by position: 4/32 in steer, 2/32 in others (U.S.).
Duals share the load; wide-base singles have no backup.
tips: Ask the driver for a photo of the sidewall size and the damage when it's safe.
Keep your fleet's tire sizes per unit type in your vendor notes.
mistakes: Ordering by "the usual size" without checking the unit.
Recording "rear tire" instead of axle, side and inside/outside.

objectives: Use a structured set of questions to clarify a complaint
Separate facts from guesses
Write a clear complaint description
body: Drivers are experts at driving — not always at describing mechanical problems. A report like "the truck is making a weird noise" is a starting point. Your job is to turn it into something a technician can act on.

timeline.title: What happened?
timeline.text: Ask the driver to describe it in their own words. What did they see, hear, smell or feel?

timeline.title: When did it start?
timeline.text: Suddenly or gradually? Today or days ago? After a specific event (hitting a pothole, fueling, a repair)?

timeline.title: Where is it?
timeline.text: Front/rear, left/right, tractor or trailer, engine area, under the cab, at the wheels?

timeline.title: Is it getting worse?
timeline.text: Constant, intermittent, or worsening? Does it happen only when braking, turning, accelerating, at speed?

timeline.title: Is the vehicle safe?
timeline.text: Can the driver control, steer and stop the vehicle normally? Is the driver in a safe location?

timeline.title: Are warning lights present?
timeline.text: Which lights or messages are on the dash? Any codes shown? Did any alarm sound?

timeline.title: Is performance affected?
timeline.text: Loss of power, speed limited, poor shifting, overheating, pulling?

callout.title: Facts, not guesses
callout.text: Drivers may say "I think it's the turbo." Record it as the driver's opinion, but describe the symptom factually: "Loud whistling from engine area under acceleration, started 30 min ago, no warning lights."

body.title: The complaint intake card
rows: Yes — truck stop, off the roadway
Air gauge drops fast when braking
body.note: Ten fields, about two minutes on the phone. Every field answers a question the vendor, dispatch or the case log will ask later.

example.title: Before and after
example.text:
Before: "Truck making weird noise."
After: "T-114 — grinding noise from front left wheel area when braking, started this morning, getting louder. No warning lights. Driver reports truck stops normally but noise is constant under braking. Currently parked at Pilot, exit 118, I-20 EB." The second version tells a vendor what to bring and tells you how urgent it is.

practical.title: Watch the interview

dialog: Okay — first, are you in a safe spot right now?
Yeah, I'm parked at a truck stop.
Good. Can you describe the noise — grinding, squealing, knocking, hissing?
Grinding. Kind of metal on metal.
When do you hear it — all the time, or when you brake, turn or accelerate?
Mostly when I brake. Front left, I think.
When did it start, and is it getting worse?
Any warning lights on the dash? And is the truck stopping normally?
No lights. It stops okay, just loud.

blocks: In under two minutes the coordinator established: safe location, type of noise, when it occurs, location on the vehicle, onset and trend, warning lights, and braking performance. Grinding during braking is a brake concern — this will be treated as urgent.

check.q: Which question should come first when a driver reports a problem?
o: What part do you think is broken?
Are you and the vehicle in a safe location?
How much will the repair cost?
Who was the last driver?
check.e: Safety first. Confirm the driver is safe before gathering technical details.

check.q: A driver says, "I think it's the alternator." How should you record this?
o: Write the complaint as "bad alternator" so the shop knows what to replace
Record the symptoms factually and note the driver's opinion separately
Leave out the driver's opinion and record only the dash lamps
Order an alternator now so the part is waiting when the truck arrives
check.e: Document observed symptoms as facts. Diagnosis is confirmed by a technician.

takeaways: Use the seven questions every time: what, when, where, trend, safety, lights, performance.
Confirm safety before technical detail.
Record symptoms as facts; label opinions as opinions.
A good complaint description tells a vendor what to bring and you how urgent it is.
tips: Read your summary back to the driver: "So — grinding, front left, when braking, since this morning. Right?"
Put a number on vague words: how many drops, how many miles, how many minutes.
mistakes: Skipping the safety question because the driver sounds calm.
Writing the driver's guess ("bad turbo") as the complaint.

deep.title: Question techniques

yes.title: Open questions — to explore
items: "What does the message on the dash say?"

blocks: Start open to let the driver describe it; switch to closed questions to pin down facts. Avoid leading questions like "It's probably the brakes, right?" — they plant answers.

objectives: Apply the seven questions to realistic calls
Extract key case data from a conversation
Recognize when an answer changes urgency
body: Real calls are messy. Drivers are stressed, tired, or on a tight schedule. Stay calm, keep questions short, and write while you listen.

tabs.label: Call 1 · Vibration

dialog: Getting a bad vibration at highway speed.
Where do you feel it — steering wheel, seat, whole truck?
Did it start suddenly? Did you hit anything?
Started after I hit a pothole an hour ago.

body: Why it matters: steering-wheel vibration after an impact points to the steer tires/wheels or front end — a steering/tire concern that should be inspected before continuing at speed.

tabs.label: Call 2 · Warning light

dialog: Got a yellow light on the dash.
Can you describe or read the symbol or message?
Any change in power, noise, smoke or temperature?

body: Why it matters: an amber check engine light with normal operation is usually not an immediate stop — but it needs a scheduled diagnosis. A red light or a stop-engine warning would change urgency completely.

tabs.label: Call 3 · Smell

dialog: I smell something hot, kind of sweet.
Is the temperature gauge normal? Any steam?
Gauge is creeping up, a little steam from the hood.
Please pull over safely as soon as possible and shut down per your training. Tell me when you're stopped.

body: Why it matters: a sweet smell plus rising temperature and steam suggests a coolant leak and overheating. Continuing could destroy the engine. This becomes an immediate roadside case.

callout.title: Answers change urgency
callout.text: Listen for words that escalate a case: "smoke," "steam," "can't stop," "pulling hard," "red light," "stop engine," "air leak," "blowout," "fire," "fluid pouring." When you hear them, prioritize safety instructions first.

stops.d: Gather details, assess, schedule or send help.
Get to a safe place; arrange prompt service.

stops.t: Smoke · steam · red lamp · air loss
stops.d: Stop safely now. Do not continue.
Emergency services first if anyone is at risk; then follow company emergency procedure.

example.title: The overlooked detail
example.text: A driver reported a "small" oil leak. The coordinator asked how small — the driver said "a few drops." The coordinator then asked whether the oil pressure gauge and warning lights were normal (yes) and scheduled an inspection at the next planned stop. A different coordinator on another call skipped the question and later learned the "small" leak was a steady stream that had already triggered a low oil pressure warning.

exercise.source:
Driver (J. Patel): Hi, this is Jay in truck 127. I'm at the Love's in Amarillo, exit 76 off I-40.
My low air warning has been coming on and off and I can hear a hissing near the back of the tractor.
It started maybe 20 minutes ago. Brakes still work but the gauge drops fast when I press the pedal.
Odometer says 412,880.

check.q: During a call the driver says, "There's smoke coming from the wheel." What is your first action?
o: Ask when the truck last had a PM so you can check the brake history
Instruct the driver to stop safely as soon as possible and follow their emergency training
Look up the nearest shop and tell the driver to head there carefully
Ask whether it is a tractor or trailer wheel so you open the right case
check.e: Smoke from a wheel end can indicate a dragging brake or failed bearing and potential fire. Safety first; details second.

check.q: An amber check engine light with no change in performance is always an immediate stop.
check.e: Usually not an immediate stop, but it needs diagnosis. Red lights, stop-engine warnings and performance changes raise urgency. Follow company procedure.

takeaways: Keep questions short and write while listening.
Escalation words — smoke, steam, can't stop, red light — change priorities instantly.
Always capture unit, location, mileage, symptom and time.
Quantify vague words like "small" or "a little".
tips: Keep a printed intake card by your phone until the questions become automatic.
If the driver is stressed, slow down your own voice — it calms the call.
mistakes: Asking for the odometer before confirming the driver is off the road.
Hanging up without telling the driver when you will call back.
