objectives: Distinguish a breakdown from a maintenance issue
Identify safety-critical defects
Know when a vehicle should not continue operating

yes.title: Maintenance issue
items: Repair can be scheduled at a convenient time/location
Examples: amber light with normal operation, minor interior issue, upcoming PM

no.title: Breakdown
items: Vehicle cannot continue — or should not
Examples: won't start, loss of brakes, blowout, severe overheating, engine shutdown

body: Some defects directly affect the ability to steer, stop, or be seen, or create fire or cargo-securement risk. These are treated as safety-critical regardless of schedule pressure.

tiles.title: Brakes
tiles.text: Air leaks, low air, brakes not releasing or dragging, brake warning lights.

tiles.title: Steering
tiles.text: Loose, hard or erratic steering; pulling; damaged steering components.

tiles.title: Tires & wheels
tiles.text: Flats, blowouts, bulges, exposed cords, loose or missing lug nuts.

tiles.title: Lighting
tiles.text: Headlights, brake lights or turn signals not working.

tiles.title: Overheating & fire risk
tiles.text: Rising temperature, steam, smoke, fuel leaks.

tiles.title: Coupling
tiles.text: Fifth wheel or kingpin problems, trailer separation risk.

callout.title: Stop criteria
callout.text: A vehicle should not continue when the driver cannot safely control, steer or stop it; when there is smoke, fire or fluid pouring; when a red stop-engine warning appears; when a tire has failed; or when a defect would place it out of service under inspection standards. When in doubt, stop safely and get a qualified technician.

body: In the United States, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration ([[FMCSA]]) sets rules for commercial vehicles, and the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance publishes [[OOS]] (out-of-service) criteria used during roadside inspections. Your company's safety department is the authority on how these apply.

body.title: The urgency matrix

items: Trailer lights out at the yard
Brake defect found on an empty unit
Brake air leak, loaded, deadline today
Derate on a loaded truck (safe location)
Parts delay on a loaded unit

body.note: Safety risk always overrides operational impact: anything in the top row does not move until a qualified technician clears it.

example.title: Pressure vs. safety
example.text: Dispatch calls: the load in T-120 is due in 3 hours and the driver says the brakes "feel soft." Dispatch asks if the driver can "just finish the run." A professional coordinator says no — brake performance complaints require inspection first — and immediately works on the fastest safe option: a mobile brake technician or the nearest capable shop, plus a recovery plan for the load.

exercise.prompt: Should the vehicle continue, or stop for service first?

items.text: Amber check engine light, truck driving normally
items.why: Needs diagnosis soon, but performance is normal. Follow company procedure.

items.text: Steer tire bulge on the sidewall
items.why: Sidewall damage on a steer tire is a blowout risk affecting steering.

items.text: Red STOP ENGINE warning with rising temperature
items.why: Red stop-engine warnings mean stop safely now to prevent damage and hazards.

items.text: Driver seat adjustment lever is loose
items.why: A comfort item that does not affect vehicle control can be scheduled.

items.text: Brake lights not working on the trailer
items.why: Following traffic cannot see the truck braking — a serious safety defect.

check.q: Which of these is a breakdown rather than a maintenance issue?
o: PM due in 2,000 miles
Tractor won't start
Sleeper light flickering
Worn floor mat
check.e: A no-start means the unit cannot operate — it requires service before it can move.

check.q: Dispatch asks you to let a driver continue with a brake issue to make an appointment. You:
o: Agree this once, since missing the appointment could lose the customer
Decline, arrange the fastest safe repair, and help dispatch plan recovery
Allow it if the driver keeps the speed low and avoids the highway
Leave it to the driver, since they can feel how the brakes are working
check.e: Safety is non-negotiable. Your job is to find the fastest safe path and help protect the load another way.

takeaways: A breakdown means the unit cannot or should not continue.
Brakes, steering, tires, lighting, overheating/fire and coupling are safety-critical.
Never pressure a driver to operate an unsafe vehicle.
Your safety department is the authority on regulatory questions.
tips: When in doubt about safety, hold the unit and get a qualified technician's opinion.
Bring dispatch a recovery option at the same time you give them bad news.
mistakes: Letting schedule pressure decide a safety question.
Treating a short distance as a reason to drive with a safety defect.

blocks.title: Can this vehicle continue?
blocks.note: Any "yes" in the first four = stop safely and get a qualified technician.

deep.title: Out-of-service basics
blocks: Roadside inspectors use the CVSA North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria. An out-of-service ([[OOS]]) vehicle defect means the vehicle cannot be operated until it is repaired. Common OOS categories include brakes, tires, lighting, coupling devices and cargo securement.

callout.title: Think like an inspector
callout.text: If a defect would put the truck out of service at a roadside inspection, it should never leave your yard with that defect.

objectives: Handle common roadside events
Give appropriate safety guidance without making mechanical decisions
Choose the right type of roadside help
body: Roadside events follow a pattern: make it safe → gather facts → get the right help → communicate. The details differ by problem.

accordion.title: Tire failure
accordion.text: Driver should pull off safely, activate hazards and place warning devices as required. Gather: position (steer/drive/trailer, left/right, inside/outside), tire size if known, wheel damage, location. Usually a mobile tire service can respond.

accordion.title: Brake problems
accordion.text: Air leaks, low air warnings, dragging or smoking brakes, poor stopping. The vehicle should stop safely and not continue until inspected by a qualified technician. Arrange mobile brake service or a tow to a capable shop.

accordion.title: Engine problems
accordion.text: Unusual noise, smoke, oil pressure warnings, stop-engine lights. Red warnings: stop safely. Gather warning messages and any fault codes displayed.

accordion.title: Overheating
accordion.text: Rising gauge, high-temperature warning, steam, sweet coolant smell. Stop safely as soon as possible — continuing can destroy the engine. Do not have drivers open a hot radiator cap.

accordion.title: Warning lights
accordion.text: Identify color and message. Amber usually means "attention needed"; red usually means "stop / serious." Note any displayed codes. Follow manufacturer and company guidance.

accordion.title: Loss of power
accordion.text: Could be a derate (engine protection) from aftertreatment, sensor or fuel issues, or a more serious failure. Is the truck safe to move to a safe location? Any messages or codes?

accordion.title: Trailer problems
accordion.text: Lights out, air leaks at glad hands, door damage, landing gear, reefer alarms. For reefer loads, temperature control is time-critical — the cargo may be at risk.

callout.title: Your role in roadside safety
callout.text: Remind drivers of safe-stop steps they are trained on (safe location, hazards, warning devices, stay clear of traffic). Do not instruct drivers to perform repairs they are not qualified or equipped for.

head: Situation
Typical help
rows: Minor air leak, light out, sensor
Engine won't run, major failure, unsafe to drive
Tow to a qualified shop / dealer
Dealer or shop with proper diagnostic tools
Reefer service + dispatch plan for cargo

items.d: Off the road, hazards, warning devices

example.title: Blowout on I-10
example.text: At 02:15 a driver reports a trailer tire blew out on I-10. The coordinator confirms the driver is safely on the shoulder with hazards on and triangles out, asks for position (trailer, rear axle, right side, outside tire) and exact location, then dispatches a 24-hour mobile tire service and updates dispatch with an ETA. The case note records every time stamp.

exercise.prompt: Choose the most appropriate first response for each event.

items.text: Trailer tire flat, truck otherwise fine, parked safely
items.why: A tire vendor can replace it on site.

items.text: Engine shut down, will not restart, knocking noise before shutdown
items.why: A serious engine failure needs a shop — do not keep trying to restart.

items.text: Trailer marker light out at a rest area
items.why: A minor lighting repair can usually be done on site.

items.text: Steering suddenly very hard and pulling after impact
items.why: A steering failure makes the vehicle unsafe to drive.

check.q: A driver reports steam from the hood and the temperature gauge rising. Best first instruction?
o: Keep driving gently to the next shop so the repair starts sooner
Stop safely as soon as possible and follow shutdown training
Pull over and open the radiator cap to check the coolant level
Turn the heater on full and keep going to help cool the engine
check.e: Overheating can destroy an engine. Stop safely. Never open a hot cooling system.

check.q: For a reefer trailer with a failed refrigeration unit, the cargo may be at risk, making the situation time-critical.
check.e: Temperature-controlled cargo can spoil — coordinate reefer service and a dispatch plan quickly.

takeaways: Roadside pattern: make it safe → gather facts → get the right help → communicate.
Match the vendor to the problem: tire service, mobile mechanic or tow.
Red warnings, overheating and brake problems mean stop safely.
Reefer failures put cargo at risk — treat as time-critical.
tips: Ask for the nearest mile marker and direction of travel — it saves vendors real time.
For reefer loads, ask for the current box temperature and set point on the first call.
mistakes: Asking drivers to attempt repairs they are not trained or equipped for.
Sending a tow before knowing whether a mobile repair could fix it.

tiles.title: Night
tiles.text: Lighting defects become critical; driver visibility on the shoulder is lower — safety instructions first.

tiles.title: Extreme cold
tiles.text: Fuel gelling, batteries, air dryer freeze-ups, DEF thawing. Driver welfare matters.

tiles.title: Extreme heat
tiles.text: Overheating, tire failures, A/C for driver health, reefer strain.

tiles.title: Storms
tiles.text: Vendors slower, tows delayed. Plan buffers and consider holding units.

items.l: alarm code on the unit display

industry.name: Thermo King
industry.text: Thermo King makes transport temperature-control systems, including refrigeration units for trailers and trucks. Its website also describes telematics temperature monitoring for reefers and a dealer network providing service across North America.
industry.relevance: When a reefer alarms, the unit's manufacturer dealer network is often the fastest route to a qualified technician — and the alarm code tells them where to start.

objectives: Sequence the first actions of a roadside breakdown
Know the warning-device requirement
Keep the driver safe while you gather information
body: The first ten minutes decide whether a breakdown stays a maintenance problem or becomes a safety incident. Drivers are trained on these steps — your job is to support them calmly and in the right order.

body.title: The first 10 minutes

rows.note: As far from traffic as possible

body.note: Illustrative sequence. U.S. rules (49 CFR 392.22) require hazard flashers immediately and warning devices within 10 minutes when a truck stops on the traveled portion or shoulder of a highway.

body.title: Tire and roadside numbers to know (U.S.)

items.l: tires on a standard five-axle tractor-trailer
minimum tread depth on other positions
to place warning devices after a stop on the road

body.note: Based on FMCSA rules (49 CFR 393.75 and 392.22). Your safety department is the authority on how they apply.

body: On a divided or one-way highway, warning devices are commonly placed about 10 feet, 100 feet and 200 feet behind the truck toward approaching traffic. On a two-lane road, placement changes so traffic in both directions is warned. Drivers are trained on the exact placement — you can remind them, not direct them.

callout.title: People before paperwork
callout.text: If anyone is hurt, the vehicle is on fire, or it is blocking live traffic, emergency services come first. Your questions can wait.

example.title: Shoulder at night
example.text: At 23:40 a driver calls from the shoulder of I-35 with a blown drive tire. The coordinator's first question is "Are your flashers on and triangles out?" The driver says he hasn't placed them yet. The coordinator says "Do that first and call me back — I'll start looking for a tire service now." Four minutes later the driver is back on the line with the mile marker.

exercise.prompt: Put the driver's first actions in order.
items: Pull as far off the roadway as possible
Call the coordinator with location and facts
Wait for help in a safe position

check.q: Under U.S. rules, how soon must warning devices be placed after a truck stops on the shoulder?
o: Within 1 hour
Within 10 minutes
Only at night
Only if the truck is loaded
check.e: 49 CFR 392.22 requires placement as soon as possible but within 10 minutes.

check.q: A driver calls from the shoulder but hasn't turned on flashers yet. You:
o: Start by taking the odometer reading and unit number for the case
Ask them to turn on flashers and place warning devices first, then call back
Tell them to keep rolling slowly to the next exit before stopping
Put them on hold and call dispatch to warn them about the delay
check.e: Safety steps first; information second.

takeaways: Flashers immediately; warning devices within 10 minutes (U.S.).
Help the driver in the right order: safe, visible, then informed.
Emergency services come first when anyone is at risk.
Remind — don't direct — trained safety procedures.
tips: Ask "Are you somewhere safe and visible?" as your very first sentence.
Offer to call back so the driver can finish safety steps.
mistakes: Taking down case details while the driver is still in a live lane.
Asking the driver to walk around a truck on a busy shoulder to read a part number.

objectives: Recite the 12 steps of the maintenance workflow
Explain the purpose of each step
Identify who is involved at each step
body: Every maintenance event — from a burned-out bulb to an engine failure — follows the same workflow. Click each step to see what happens and why it matters.

callout.title: Company procedure rules
callout.text: Approval limits, preferred vendors and documentation systems differ between companies. The workflow stays the same — the details inside each step follow your company's procedure.

example.title: Where cases go wrong
example.text: Most problems come from skipping steps: not determining urgency (a brake issue gets treated like a light bulb), not confirming the repair (the driver leaves and the problem returns in 50 miles), or not documenting (next month nobody knows the same part was replaced before).

exercise.prompt: Arrange the steps in the correct order.

check.q: What comes immediately after gathering information from the driver?
o: Find a vendor
Determine urgency
Close the case
Communicate ETA
check.e: Urgency decides everything that follows — how fast, which vendor, whether the unit can move.

check.q: A case can be closed as soon as the shop says the repair is done.
check.e: Confirm the repair — that the complaint is resolved and the driver has the unit — and document before closing.

takeaways: Twelve steps: report → gather → urgency → vendor → arrival → diagnosis → repair → track → ETA → confirm → document → close.
Urgency drives vendor choice and speed.
Confirm the repair before closing.
Procedure details vary; the workflow does not.

blocks.title: Example internal response targets (minutes)
items: Dispatch notified of new down unit
blocks.note: Example targets — many fleets set internal service levels like these to keep cases moving.

objectives: Follow a real case through the full workflow
See how communication and documentation happen at each step
Identify decision points
body: Here is a complete case, time-stamped as it would appear in a case log.

timeline.title: 10:02 · Driver reports issue
timeline.text: Driver in T-133 reports ABS warning light on the trailer (TR-518) after coupling. Parked at customer in Memphis, TN.

timeline.title: 10:05 · Gather information
timeline.text: Light stays on after restart; no braking issues felt; trailer loaded; odometer noted; case opened on TR-518.

timeline.title: 10:08 · Determine urgency
timeline.text: ABS is a brake-system warning. Per procedure: urgent — inspect before long-distance travel.

timeline.title: 10:15 · Find vendor
timeline.text: Mobile mechanic with trailer ABS diagnostic capability, 35-minute ETA.

timeline.title: 10:55 · Coordinate arrival
timeline.text: Tech on site. Driver confirmed contact.

timeline.title: 11:20 · Obtain diagnosis
timeline.text: Damaged ABS sensor connector at right rear wheel. Estimate provided.

timeline.title: 11:25 · Coordinate repair
timeline.text: Estimate within coordinator approval limit per procedure. Approved; PO issued.

timeline.title: 11:30 · Track & communicate ETA
timeline.text: ETR 12:00. Dispatch updated: departure delayed ~90 minutes.

timeline.title: 12:05 · Confirm repair
timeline.text: Tech confirms light off after test. Driver confirms light off.

timeline.title: 12:10 · Document & close
timeline.text: Notes, invoice, parts, labor, times and downtime recorded. Case closed.

callout.title: Notice the time stamps
callout.text: Downtime for this case = 10:02 to 12:05 ≈ 2 hours. Accurate time stamps make downtime reporting possible.

body.title: Case TR-518: where the two hours went
body.note: The 5-minute approval is what good looks like — the estimate was within the coordinator's limit and approved immediately.

body.title: The decision points in one case

items.d: Tractor or trailer — opens the right case

body.note: Each decision is also a documentation point: write down what you decided, when, and why.

example.title: Decision point: approval
example.text: At 11:25 the estimate was within the coordinator's limit. Had the shop recommended replacing all trailer brake chambers for a much higher amount, the coordinator would route it for approval per procedure — and ask whether the additional work was required now for safety or could be scheduled.

exercise.prompt: At 11:30, which message to dispatch is best?

options.why: No unit, no cause, no ETA — dispatch can't plan with this.

options.text: "TR-518 (with T-133) — ABS sensor connector being repaired on site. ETR 12:00. Expect departure ~12:15, about 90 min behind plan. Will confirm when released."
options.why: Unit, cause, ETR, impact and next update — everything dispatch needs.

options.text: "Should be done soon, I'll let you know."
options.why: Vague and gives no time for planning.

check.q: In the example, why was the case opened on TR-518 instead of T-133?
o: The driver requested it
The ABS warning was for the trailer
T-133 was not in the system
Tractors don't have ABS
check.e: The fault belonged to the trailer. Cases are opened on the unit that has the problem.

check.q: Which step produces the data needed to calculate downtime?
o: Accurate time stamps throughout the case
The vendor's final invoice, which lists the repair hours
The dispatcher's notes about when the load was replanned
The fleet manager's approval of the final estimate
check.e: Downtime is calculated from time stamps — when the unit went down and when it was released.

takeaways: A strong case log is time-stamped at every step.
Communicate cause, ETR and impact — not just "it's getting fixed."
Approval decisions follow company limits and procedures.
Confirm with both the technician and the driver before closing.
tips: Log a time stamp at every step — the timeline builds itself.
Ask the vendor to call you the moment diagnosis is done, not when the repair is.
mistakes: Letting approval become the longest bar on the timeline.
Recording "morning" instead of an actual time.

objectives: Apply the principles of clear maintenance communication
Communicate calmly and helpfully with drivers
Give dispatch the information they need to plan

tiles.title: Specific
tiles.text: Unit numbers, locations, times, names. Not "soon" or "the truck."

tiles.title: Timely
tiles.text: Update when something changes — before someone has to ask.

tiles.title: Honest
tiles.text: If you don't know, say so, and say when you will know.

tiles.title: Respectful
tiles.text: Drivers are stranded, dispatchers are under pressure. Calm and courteous wins.

body: A broken-down driver is often stressed, losing pay time, and worried about safety. Acknowledge the situation, give clear next steps, and tell them when they will hear from you.

msg.title: Good — message to driver
msg.text: Hi Marcus — a mobile tire tech from Southwest Tire is on the way, ETA 45 min (around 3:30). Tech's name is Luis, he'll call when close. Stay safe off the roadway. I'll check back at 3:30 if I haven't heard from you.

body: Dispatch plans loads around your information. Always include: unit, status, cause (short), ETR, impact, and when you will update next.

msg.title: Good — update to dispatch
msg.text: T-114 update: at Lone Star Truck Center Dallas for a coolant leak. Diagnosis: water pump. Part in stock. ETR today 16:00. Load 48213 will miss the 14:00 pickup — recommend reschedule or recovery truck. Next update 13:00.

example.title: Handling a frustrated driver
example.text: A driver says, "This is the third time this truck has broken down this month. I'm losing money!" A professional response acknowledges and acts: "I understand, that's frustrating — I see the two earlier cases in the history. I'm getting you help now, and I'm also flagging this as a repeat issue so we look for the root cause." Then follow through.

exercise.prompt: Dispatch messages: "Is 127 going to make its 18:00 delivery?" The shop said the repair should finish at 17:30 and the delivery is 40 minutes away. Best reply?

options.why: Overconfident — it hides the risk and gives dispatch no chance to prepare.

options.text: "Shop ETR is 17:30; delivery is ~40 min away, so arrival ~18:10 at best. It will likely be late — recommend calling the receiver now. I'll confirm as soon as it's released."
options.why: Shares facts, the math, the risk and a recommendation.

check.q: Which set of details should every dispatch update include?
o: Unit, status, cause, ETR, impact, next update
Unit, driver name, shop address and invoice total
Status, weather, the driver's mood and the vendor's phone
Cause, part numbers, labor rate and warranty terms
check.e: These six elements let dispatch plan without calling you back.

check.q: If you don't know an ETR, it is best to give an optimistic estimate so dispatch isn't worried.
check.e: Be honest: say you don't know yet and when you expect to know.

takeaways: Be specific, timely, honest and respectful.
Drivers need clear next steps and a check-back time.
Dispatch updates: unit, status, cause, ETR, impact, next update.
Never guess an ETR to make someone feel better.
tips: Use the same structure every time — dispatchers learn to read your updates in seconds.
If nothing changed, still send the update at the promised time: "No change, next update 15:00."
mistakes: "Soon" and "should be fine" instead of times.
Waiting until the ETR is missed to tell anyone it will be missed.

blocks.title: Phone vs text vs email
blocks.hint: Rule of thumb: call for anything urgent or safety-related, then confirm in writing.

yes.title: Sounds professional
items: "Here's what I know, and when I'll know more."

no.title: Sounds unprofessional
items: "Why didn't you check that?" (in the moment)

objectives: Communicate complaint details to shops effectively
Work professionally with parts vendors
Report to fleet managers and management concisely

tabs.label: Shops & technicians
body: Give the shop everything it needs to start working immediately: unit and VIN, mileage, complaint in factual terms, any codes, what was already done, authorization rules and billing information.

msg.title: Repair request to shop
msg.text:
Unit: T-114 (VIN ending 48213) · Odometer 512,340
Complaint: Coolant leak, front of engine. Temp rose to warning level before driver stopped. No codes reported.
History: Water pump replaced 14 months ago (warranty may apply).
Please call with diagnosis and estimate before repairs beyond diagnosis.
PO to follow upon approval. Contact: [Coordinator] ext. 204

tabs.label: Parts vendors
body: When sourcing parts, be precise: part number (if known), VIN, engine or component serial, quantity, needed-by time, delivery location. Ask about availability, price, core charges and lead time.

msg.title: Parts inquiry
msg.text: Looking for a water pump for a 2021 tractor, VIN attached. Need delivery to Lone Star Dallas by 13:00 if possible. Please confirm price, core charge (if any), and availability.

tabs.label: Fleet managers
body: Fleet managers want the decision, the cost and the risk — not every detail. Lead with the ask.

msg.title: Approval request
msg.text: Approval needed: T-114 water pump replacement — $1,475 (parts $620, labor 4.5 h @ $190). Unit down since 08:10. Pump replaced 14 months ago — checking warranty with the dealer. ETR 16:00 if approved by 11:00.

tabs.label: Management
body: Senior management typically wants summaries: how many units are down, why, the impact on customers, and what you need from them. Use bullets and numbers.

msg.title: End-of-day summary
msg.text:
Fleet status — 5 units down (4.0% of fleet)
• 2 waiting on parts (ETAs tomorrow)
• 2 in repair (ETR tonight)
• 1 roadside tire (resolved, rolling)
Customer impact: 1 late delivery (recovered by T-140).
Risk: T-120 third aftertreatment failure in 60 days — recommending root-cause review.

callout.title: Match the audience
callout.text: Technicians want detail. Managers want decisions. Drivers want next steps. Dispatch wants time. Same case — different message.

items.l: Driver — what happens now and when you'll call
Manager — the ask, cost and risk

body.title: Everyone you talk to on one repair
A complete hand-off to a shop
rows: Grinding front left when braking, started this morning
Pulls slightly left; no warning lamps
Diagnose only — call before any repair
Check — brake job here 3 months ago
Your name, direct line, update by 11:00
body.note: A shop that gets this up front doesn't need to call you back with questions — and doesn't start unapproved work.

example.title: The missing detail
example.text: A coordinator sent a truck to a shop with the note "check engine light." The shop spent an hour on diagnosis before discovering the driver had also reported intermittent power loss and a failed regeneration — details that were in the coordinator's notes but not in the request. Including them would have pointed diagnosis toward aftertreatment immediately.

exercise.prompt: Who is each message written for?

items.text: "Codes SPN 3251 / FMI 0 reported, regen attempted twice, failed. Please call before exceeding diagnosis."
items.why: Technical detail and authorization rules are for the shop.

items.text: "Need approval: $2,300 DPF cleaning + sensor. Down 2 days if we wait for dealer. Recommend approve."
items.why: Decision, cost, trade-off and recommendation — manager format.

items.text: "Tow is 40 min out. Stay in the cab, hazards on. I'll call you at 4:15."
items.why: Clear next steps, safety and check-back time.

check.q: What should a request to a shop always include regarding authorization?
o: Nothing; the shop decides which repairs are needed and bills for them
Instructions to call with diagnosis and estimate before additional repairs
Permission to do any repair the technician finds, to save time
The driver's phone number so the shop can get approval from them
check.e: Clear authorization rules prevent surprise charges and follow company approval procedures.

check.q: A fleet manager asks about a repair. What should you lead with?
o: Full transcript of the driver call
The decision needed, cost, and impact
The shop's history
Your opinion of the dispatcher
check.e: Managers need decision-ready information first; details on request.

takeaways: Shops need complete, factual complaint details and authorization rules.
Parts inquiries need VIN/part numbers, quantity, location and timing.
Managers want the decision, cost and risk first.
Tailor every message to its audience.
tips: Lead with the one thing the reader needs, then add detail.
Put authorization rules in writing on every shop request.
mistakes: Sending a technical paragraph to a manager who needs one decision.
Forwarding a whole message thread instead of summarizing it.

objectives: Identify the key elements of maintenance documentation
Understand work orders and repair history
Record mileage, engine hours and times correctly
body: If it isn't documented, it didn't happen. Documentation is how the company knows what was done to each unit, what it cost, and whether problems are repeating.

body: Financial and time details turn case notes into data the company can manage.

objectives: Explain pre-trip and post-trip inspections
Follow a DVIR defect from report to certified repair
Know where the coordinator fits in the loop
body: Every day, drivers inspect their equipment. When they find a defect, it goes on a Driver Vehicle Inspection Report ([[DVIR]]). Many of your cases start on that piece of paper — or its electronic version.

body.title: The DVIR repair loop
body.note: Based on FMCSA 49 CFR 396.11 and 396.13. Your safety department defines exactly how your company completes each step.

tiles.title: Brakes & air system
tiles.text: Service and parking brakes, air lines, audible leaks.

tiles.title: Steering
tiles.text: Steering mechanism and play.

tiles.title: Lighting & reflectors
tiles.text: Headlights, brake lights, turn signals, markers.

tiles.title: Tires, wheels & rims
tiles.text: Inflation, damage, lug nuts.

tiles.title: Coupling devices
tiles.text: Fifth wheel, kingpin, safety devices.

tiles.title: Emergency equipment
tiles.text: Warning devices, fire extinguisher, and wipers/mirrors among others.

callout.title: The coordinator's part
callout.text: Turn each DVIR defect into a case, get it repaired before the unit is dispatched when it affects safety, and make sure the repair is documented so the next driver can review and sign off.

body: U.S. rules require a written post-trip report of defects that would affect safe operation or cause a breakdown. Before driving, the next driver must review the last report and confirm that listed defects were repaired or that repair wasn't needed. Exact forms and electronic systems differ — your safety department owns the procedure.

body.title: Pre-trip vs post-trip inspection

items.sub: Before the vehicle is driven.
facts: Driver must be satisfied the vehicle is in safe condition and review the last DVIR (49 CFR 396.13)
items.watch: Defects found here can stop a dispatch — the earlier you hear, the more options you have.

items.sub: At the end of the day's work.
facts: A written DVIR is required when a defect is found or reported (49 CFR 396.11, property carriers)
items.watch: Post-trip defects are your overnight work list — schedule them before the unit's next dispatch.

body.key: Pre-trip protects today's trip; post-trip feeds tonight's repairs. Both land on the coordinator's desk.

body.title: How a reported defect is handled

stops.d: Record it and schedule the repair.
Repair (and certify) before the vehicle operates again.
The vehicle may not move until repaired.

body.note: Your safety department decides how defects are classified. The coordinator's job is to get each one repaired and certified on time.

example.title: The marker light that stopped a dispatch
example.text: A post-trip DVIR listed "left marker light out" on TR-532. The coordinator opened a case, a yard technician replaced the bulb that evening, and the repair was certified on the DVIR. The morning driver reviewed and signed it — the trailer left on time instead of being held at the gate.

check.q: What must the next driver do with the previous DVIR?
o: Nothing, as long as the truck passes their own pre-trip inspection
Review it and confirm defects were repaired or not needing repair

Send it to the customer along with the delivery paperwork
check.e: Drivers review the last report before driving (49 CFR 396.13).

check.q: A DVIR defect that affects safe operation should be repaired before the vehicle is dispatched.
check.e: Safety-affecting defects are repaired (and certified) before the vehicle operates again.

takeaways: DVIRs are a major source of maintenance cases.
Safety-affecting defects are fixed before dispatch.
Repairs are certified so the next driver can sign off.
Your safety department owns the exact procedure.
tips: Review new DVIRs at the start and end of each shift.
Close the loop with the yard so certified repairs are visible to the next driver.
mistakes: Treating DVIR comments as "just notes".
Fixing the defect but never documenting the repair on the DVIR.

objectives: Describe what maintenance records must show
Understand roadside inspection levels and out-of-service outcomes
Explain how inspections affect the company's safety record
body: Maintenance records prove equipment is maintained. Roadside inspections test that claim in the real world — and the results follow the company.

body.title: Key U.S. record requirements (summary)
head: Record
What it shows
Kept for
rows: Unit ID, inspection & maintenance schedule, record of inspections, repairs and maintenance
Where the vehicle is housed for 1 year, and 6 months after it leaves the carrier's control
That the unit passed its periodic inspection
body.note: Summarized from 49 CFR 396.3, 396.11 and 396.21. Rules change and have exceptions — your safety department is the authority.

body.title: CVSA roadside inspection levels
head: Level
Name
What's checked
rows: Driver documents and a full vehicle inspection, including under the vehicle
Driver documents and vehicle items checkable without going under it
Driver credentials, hours of service, documents
A one-time examination of a particular item
Full vehicle inspection without the driver present
A state or provincial program that does not meet any other level; no CVSA decal
Data checked wirelessly while the vehicle is moving, with no officer contact
body.note: A vehicle that passes a Level I, V or VI inspection with no critical violations may receive a CVSA decal, valid for up to three months.

body: Roadside inspection results feed the FMCSA's Compliance, Safety, Accountability program ([[CSA]]). Vehicle violations count toward the Vehicle Maintenance category (one of seven "BASICs"). Poor scores can lead to more inspections and interventions. Every defect you fix before it reaches the road helps the company's record.

body.title: Most common vehicle out-of-service violations, U.S., fiscal year 2025
items: Tire flat, leaking or under 50% pressure
body.note: Out-of-service orders from FMCSA roadside inspection data, as published in public FY2025 summaries; counts are approximate. Tires, brakes and lights are also the items a good DVIR and pre-trip catch first.

body.h: After a roadside inspection: closing the report

body: Every roadside inspection ends with a report, even a clean one. When the inspector lists violations, the report starts a paper trail the company must close. The driver hands it in at the next terminal or as company procedure says. Most fleets ask for a photo the same day.

body.title: Closing a roadside inspection report

items.d: Photo from the driver, same day
Out-of-service items before the unit moves

body.note: Based on 49 CFR 396.9. The form says where to send it. Your safety department signs it or tells you who does.

head: When
What the coordinator does
rows: Get a clear photo of the whole report. Open a case for every vehicle violation, including ones that are not out of service.
Repair every out-of-service item. Send a mobile repair to the unit, or a tow. Keep the work order.
A carrier official signs the report to certify that every violation was fixed, then returns it as the form directs. Attach or file the repair orders.
Keep a copy of the certified report.
The safety team can ask FMCSA to review inspection data through its free DataQs system. Give them the repair records, photos and times.

callout.title: Out of service means parked
callout.text: A vehicle placed out of service may not be driven until the listed repairs are done (49 CFR 396.9(c)). That includes "just to the next exit." Bring the repair to the unit, or tow it.

exercise.prompt: A driver sends a photo of a roadside report: trailer brake out of adjustment, marked out of service. Put your steps in order.
items: Confirm the unit is parked safely and stays parked
Send a brake-qualified mobile technician to the unit
Get the repair order showing the brake was fixed and adjusted
Have a carrier official sign the report within 15 days and return it as the form directs
File a copy of the certified report for 12 months

example.title: Cheap bulb, expensive violation
example.text: A $4 bulb out on a trailer led to a Level II inspection and a violation on the company's record. After reviewing a quarter's inspections, the coordinator started a "lights and air" check at every trailer drop — lighting violations fell sharply the next quarter.

items.text: Inspector checks the driver's documents and walks around the truck without going underneath
items.why: Walk-Around inspection.

items.text: Full vehicle inspection including under the vehicle, plus driver documents
items.why: North American Standard Inspection.

items.text: Only the driver's license, medical card and hours of service are checked
items.why: Driver-Only inspection.

check.q: Which CSA category do vehicle defect violations mainly affect?
o: Unsafe Driving
Vehicle Maintenance
Driver Fitness
Crash Indicator
check.e: Vehicle defects count toward the Vehicle Maintenance BASIC.

check.q: Periodic (annual) inspection reports must be kept for 14 months under U.S. rules.
check.e: 49 CFR 396.21 requires retention for 14 months.

check.q: A roadside inspection lists two vehicle violations. How long does the carrier have to certify they were fixed?
o: 24 hours
15 days
30 days
Until the next annual inspection
check.e: Under 49 CFR 396.9(d), a carrier official certifies that the violations were corrected within 15 days of the inspection, and the carrier keeps a copy for 12 months.

check.q: A truck placed out of service at a roadside inspection may drive slowly to the nearest shop.
check.e: An out-of-service vehicle may not be driven until the repairs are done (49 CFR 396.9(c)). Send a mobile repair, or tow it.

takeaways: Maintenance records must show inspections, repairs and schedules.
CVSA levels range from full inspections to driver-only.
Violations affect the company's CSA record.
Tires, brakes and lights cause most vehicle out-of-service orders, and most are preventable.
A roadside report with violations is certified within 15 days and kept for 12 months.
tips: Review roadside inspection reports weekly and open cases for every vehicle violation.
Track violations by unit and by category.
Ask drivers for a photo of every inspection report, clean ones too. A clean inspection is good news to share.
mistakes: Assuming a clean inspection means the unit is fine for months.
Losing inspection paperwork that proves repairs were made.
